Gene Description

MYD88 (myeloid differentiation primary response protein 88) is a cytosolic signaling adaptor of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) and interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R) families. It has an N-terminal death domain, a short intermediate domain and a C-terminal TIR domain. Ligand-activated TLRs (all except TLR3) and IL-1, IL-18, IL-33 and IL-36 receptors recruit MYD88 through TIR-TIR contacts, either directly or via the bridging adaptor TIRAP at the plasma membrane (TLR2, TLR4). At endosomes it serves TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9. MYD88 death domains then oligomerise and recruit IRAK4 and IRAK1/IRAK2 into a helical signaling platform, the Myddosome. In the Myddosome IRAK4 is activated and TRAF6 is engaged, which leads to NF-kappa-B and MAP kinase activation, inflammatory cytokine production and, in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, IRF7-dependent type I interferon production. MYD88 has no known enzymatic activity. It is regulated by K63- and K11-linked ubiquitination and by deubiquitinases such as USP3 and OTUD5. Inherited MYD88 deficiency causes susceptibility to pyogenic bacterial infection. The recurrent somatic L265P mutation constitutively activates the pathway in B-cell lymphomas.

GO:0008063 Toll signaling pathway
IBA
GO_REF:0000033 		MODIFY
Summary: IBA (PTN000386853, donors fly Myd88 and rat Myd88): Toll signaling pathway.
Reason: GO:0008063 is defined for ligand binding to "the receptor Toll" and is not an ancestor of GO:0002224 toll-like receptor signaling pathway (checked in OLS). The IBD at the MyD88 node correctly captures an ancestral adaptor role in Toll-family receptor signaling, but human MYD88 functions downstream of vertebrate TLRs and IL-1R family receptors, not Toll. The vertebrate-appropriate term is GO:0002755.
Propagation Review
Root cause: TERM SCOPING PROBLEM
Failure modes: LINEAGE OR TAXON MISMATCH GRANULARITY MISMATCH
Sources checked:
PANTHER:PTN000386853 · PTN000386853 SUPPORTS SOURCE BUT NOT TARGET
The MyD88-family node carries both GO:0008063 (seeded from fly Myd88 and rat Myd88) and the vertebrate TLR terms. The ancestral adaptor role in Toll-family receptor signalling is sound, but GO:0008063 names the Drosophila Toll receptor pathway and is not an ancestor of GO:0002224, so for vertebrate descendants the TLR pathway term is the correct scope.
Proposed replacements: MyD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling pathway

Understanding early TLR signaling through the Myddosome. 		ACCEPT
Summary: NAS (Myddosome review): serine/threonine protein kinase complex.
Reason: The Myddosome contains the IRAK4 and IRAK1/2 kinases with MYD88 as its scaffold; GO has no specific Myddosome term, so this is the most specific available complex term.
Supporting Evidence:
PMID:30256449
Upon activation, TLRs facilitate the assembly of large intracellular oligomeric signaling complexes, termed Myddosomes, which initiate key signal transduction pathways to elicit critical inflammatory immune responses.
PMID:36865541
The myddosome is a supramolecular signaling complex assembled upon dimerization of IL-1Rs and most TLRs (except TLR3), and is composed of MyD88, IRAK4, IRAK1 and/or IRAK2, in addition to TRAF6.

Core Functions

Signaling adaptor that couples ligand-activated TLRs (all except TLR3) to the IRAK kinases: MYD88 is recruited through its TIR domain (directly, or via TIRAP for TLR2/TLR4) and nucleates the Myddosome through death-domain oligomerisation.

Molecular Function:
signaling adaptor activity
Directly Involved In:
MyD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling pathway
Cellular Locations:
extrinsic component of cytoplasmic side of plasma membrane cytosol
Supporting Evidence:
  • PMID:9734363
    our findings implicate MyD88 as a general adaptor/regulator molecule for the Toll/IL-1R family of receptors for innate immunity.
  • PMID:16751103
    TIRAP then functions to facilitate MyD88 delivery to activated TLR4 to initiate signal transduction.
  • PMID:38961291
    within most myddosomes, MyD88 forms barrel-like structures that function as scaffolds for effector protein recruitment.

Suggested Questions for Experts

Q: Should GO:0008063 Toll signaling pathway be removed from the MyD88-family IBD at PTN000386853 for vertebrate descendants, or restricted to the arthropod clade? GO:0008063 is defined for the receptor Toll and is not an ancestor of GO:0002224, so all vertebrate MYD88 orthologues currently inherit a Drosophila-specific pathway term.

Q: Human MYD88 is the adaptor for IL-18R1/IL18RAP signalling, but neither human MYD88 nor IRAK4 or TRAF6 is annotated to GO:0035655 interleukin-18-mediated signaling pathway (only ligand, receptor and a few kinases are). Is this a deliberate convention or a gap for the adaptor layer?

Q: The mouse Myd88 annotations to GO:0140674 ATP-dependent histone chaperone activity and GO:0006325 chromatin organization (IMP, PMID:18319258) read an indirect transcriptional phenotype as a molecular activity; should the MGI source annotations be withdrawn so that they stop propagating to human and other orthologues?

Q: Which reference supports the IEP annotation to GO:0071260 cellular response to mechanical stimulus? The cited PMID:19593445 does not mention MyD88.

Q: Would a Myddosome cellular-component term (MYD88-IRAK4-IRAK1/2 helical assembly) be useful? GO:1902554 serine/threonine protein kinase complex is currently the most specific available term.

Suggested Experiments

Experiment: Endogenous-tag proteomics (as in PMID:38961291) comparing Myddosome composition after IL-18, IL-33 and IL-36 stimulation with TLR stimulation, to test whether the MYD88 scaffold recruits the same effector set across IL-1R family receptors.

Experiment: Genome-edited human macrophages lacking MYD88 (not siRNA), to test whether any phagocytosis defect exists independently of TLR4-TRAM signalling. Human siRNA and mouse knockout data currently disagree.

Experiment: Chromatin immunoprecipitation or CUT&RUN for endogenous MYD88, with a nuclear-exclusion mutant, to test whether the reported nuclear pool has any direct role at promoters or is an overexpression artefact.

Comprehensive Research Report: Human MYD88 (Myeloid Differentiation Primary Response Protein 88)

Gene Identity Verification

The research target has been confirmed as human MYD88 (UniProt: Q99836), encoding the myeloid differentiation primary response protein MyD88. The protein contains the expected domain architecture including a DEATH-like domain superfamily region, Death domain (IPR000488), MyD88 Death domain (IPR034249), and TIR domain (IPR000157), consistent with the UniProt annotation for Homo sapiens (song2024myd88andits pages 1-2, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2).

1. Primary Function and Molecular Mechanism

1.1 Core Adaptor Function

Human MYD88 functions as a critical cytoplasmic adaptor protein that links activated innate immune receptors—particularly Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and interleukin-1 receptor family members (IL-1R, IL-18R)—to downstream signaling kinases and transcription factors (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4, song2024myd88andits pages 1-2, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6). Unlike enzymes that catalyze biochemical reactions with specific substrates, MYD88 operates as a non-enzymatic scaffold protein that organizes proximity-driven signaling complexes (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2).

MYD88 mediates signaling from nearly all TLRs except TLR3, which uses the alternative TRIF adaptor (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 3-5, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6). Following receptor engagement by pathogen-associated or damage-associated molecular patterns, MYD88 is recruited to the receptor's intracellular TIR domain and nucleates formation of a supramolecular organizing center called the "myddosome" (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 2-4).

1.2 Structural Organization and Domain Functions

MYD88 consists of three functionally distinct domains that cooperate to transduce receptor signals:

MYD88 region Approximate residues in human MYD88L Structural characteristics Primary function in signaling Key experimental or mechanistic features
N-terminal death domain (DD) 1–109; experimentally defined folded core approximately Arg20–Ala104 Death-domain superfamily module specialized for homotypic and heterotypic protein–protein interactions Oligomerizes with other MYD88 DDs and recruits the DDs of IRAK4, followed by IRAK1 and/or IRAK2, thereby building the kinase-recruiting core of the myddosome MYD88 DD oligomerization determines myddosome architecture. MYD88 and IRAK DDs form a layered, left-handed helical assembly that promotes IRAK4 trans-autophosphorylation and downstream IRAK1/2 activation; reported complexes commonly contain approximately 6–8 MYD88 and four IRAK4 molecules (gurkan2024theirakmdeath pages 1-2, pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 2-4, gurkan2024theirakmdeath pages 8-10)
Intermediate domain (ID/INT) 110–155; approximately 46 amino acids Largely intrinsically disordered linker between the DD and TIR domain, with transient secondary structure Supports productive myddosome nucleation, complex growth, IRAK4 recruitment or activation, and NF-κB signal propagation; it is therefore more than a passive linker Residues Gln114–Leu118, especially Tyr116, are critical for productive myddosome assembly. The short splice isoform MYD88S, which lacks this region, can enter nascent complexes but prevents their maturation and acts as a dominant-negative regulator (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 2-4, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 9-11)
C-terminal Toll/interleukin-1 receptor domain (TIR) 156–296 Flavodoxin-like TIR fold containing signaling surfaces and a functionally important BB loop Engages TIR domains of activated Toll-like and IL-1 receptor-family receptors, either directly or through TIRAP/MAL, and nucleates higher-order MYD88 assembly at receptor-proximal signaling sites Recent structural work shows two offset, parallel, head-to-tail MYD88-TIR strands stabilized by asymmetric BE intrastrand and BCD interstrand interfaces. A 2024 TLR2-nucleated MicroED structure resolved this assembly at 2.85 Å and revealed signaling-associated rearrangements in the B helix, BB loop, and CD loop (bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 2-3, bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 7-8, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 1-2, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 8-11)
Integrated full-length architecture 1–296 Modular DD–ID–TIR adaptor; not an enzyme and has no catalytic substrate Converts receptor activation into proximity-driven assembly of the MYD88–IRAK4–IRAK1/2 myddosome, ultimately activating NF-κB, MAPK/AP-1, and receptor-context-dependent IRF signaling Functional sequence: receptor TIR engagement → cooperative MYD88-TIR assembly → DD-mediated myddosome formation → IRAK recruitment and activation → TRAF6–TAK1 signaling. The oncogenic L265P substitution lies in the TIR domain and promotes constitutive aggregation and signaling (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, vegivinti2023roleofinnate pages 1-3, song2024myd88andits pages 1-2, minderman2023theoncogenichuman pages 8-9)

Table: This table maps the three principal domains of human MYD88L to their approximate residue boundaries, structural properties, and signaling functions. It also summarizes experimental evidence connecting each region to receptor recruitment, myddosome assembly, and downstream signal propagation.

N-terminal Death Domain (DD; residues ~1-109): The death domain mediates homotypic protein-protein interactions with other MYD88 molecules and heterotypic interactions with the death domains of IL-1 receptor-associated kinases (IRAKs), particularly IRAK4 and IRAK1/2 (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, gurkan2024theirakmdeath pages 1-2). Through these interactions, the DD constructs the core oligomeric scaffold of the myddosome. Structural studies reveal that the myddosome assembles as a layered, left-handed helical complex typically containing approximately 6-8 MyD88 molecules associating with four IRAK4 molecules (pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 2-4, gurkan2024theirakmdeath pages 8-10).

Intermediate Domain (ID; residues ~110-155): Initially thought to be merely a passive linker, the 46-amino-acid intermediate domain is largely intrinsically disordered yet plays an essential regulatory role in myddosome nucleation and signal propagation (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 2-4). Residues Gln114-Leu118, particularly Tyr116, are critical for productive myddosome assembly and IRAK4 activation (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 2-4, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 12-14, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 9-11). The alternatively spliced isoform MyD88S, which lacks the intermediate domain, can be incorporated into nascent signaling complexes but prevents their maturation, thereby acting as a dominant-negative regulator that terminates inflammatory signaling (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 9-11).

C-terminal TIR Domain (residues ~156-296): The Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain adopts a flavodoxin-like fold and engages the TIR domains of activated receptors, either directly or through bridging adaptors such as TIRAP/MAL (saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 2-4, bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 2-3, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6). The TIR domain's BB loop is functionally critical for TIR-TIR homotypic interactions that drive MyD88 oligomerization (saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 2-4).

1.3 Mechanism of Myddosome Assembly

Recent structural and mechanistic studies have elucidated the stepwise process of myddosome formation:

  1. Receptor Nucleation: Ligand-induced receptor dimerization or oligomerization triggers conformational changes in receptor cytoplasmic TIR domains, creating high-affinity binding sites for MYD88 TIR domains (pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 2-4, song2024myd88andits pages 2-4).

  2. TIR-Domain Assembly: MYD88 TIR domains assemble into two-stranded, parallel, head-to-tail filamentous structures. A landmark 2024 microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED) study resolved the TLR2-nucleated MyD88 TIR assembly at 2.85 Å resolution, revealing that assembly is stabilized by asymmetric intrastrand BE interfaces and lateral interstrand BCD interfaces (li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 8-11, bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 7-8, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 1-2). The EE surface of incoming MyD88 molecules binds the BB surface of already-oligomerized subunits, driving conformational rearrangement of the B helix and BB loop and supporting unidirectional elongation (li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 8-11).

  3. Progressive Oligomerization: MyD88 molecules initially form small, unstable oligomers that grow progressively with continued receptor stimulation (pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 2-4, song2024myd88andits pages 2-4). Once the oligomer reaches a critical size threshold, it establishes stable interactions with IRAK4 (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4).

  4. IRAK Recruitment and Activation: The assembled MyD88 death domains recruit four IRAK4 molecules, followed by IRAK1 and/or IRAK2, creating a three-layered helical signaling complex (gurkan2024theirakmdeath pages 1-2, pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 2-4, gurkan2024theirakmdeath pages 8-10). Proximity within this structure enables IRAK4 molecules to trans-autophosphorylate and subsequently phosphorylate and activate IRAK1/2 (pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 2-4, vegivinti2023roleofinnate pages 1-3).

  5. Downstream Signaling Initiation: Activated IRAK1 dissociates from the myddosome and engages the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRAF6, initiating the downstream TAK1-IKK-NF-κB and MAPK cascades (vegivinti2023roleofinnate pages 1-3, pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 6-7).

2. Subcellular Localization

MYD88 is a cytoplasmic/cytosolic protein that carries out its signaling function at receptor-associated sites (song2024myd88andits pages 1-2, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2). In its basal state, MYD88 resides in the cytoplasm. Upon receptor activation, it is recruited to the intracellular domains of TLRs and IL-1R family members at cellular membranes, where it assembles into functional myddosome signaling complexes (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 1-2, pustelny2022mechanismofmyd88s pages 11-12). The myddosome forms at membrane-proximal sites for plasma-membrane receptors (TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, IL-1R) or at endosomal membranes for intracellular TLRs (TLR7, TLR8, TLR9) that detect nucleic acids (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6).

MYD88 functions downstream of most TLRs and the IL-1 receptor family:

Direct MYD88 Recruitment: TLR5, TLR7, TLR8, TLR9, IL-1R, and IL-18R directly recruit MYD88 through TIR-domain interactions (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 3-5, song2024myd88andits pages 1-2).

TIRAP/MAL-Mediated Recruitment: TLR1/2, TLR2/6, and TLR4 require the bridging adaptor TIRAP (also called MAL) to facilitate MYD88 recruitment (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 3-5).

TLR4 Dual Signaling: TLR4 is unique in engaging both MYD88-dependent and MYD88-independent pathways. At the plasma membrane, TLR4 signals through TIRAP-MYD88 to activate early NF-κB and inflammatory cytokines. After endocytosis, TLR4 switches to a TRAM-TRIF pathway that activates IRF3, type I interferons, and late NF-κB signaling (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 3-5).

TLR3 Exception: TLR3 is the only TLR that does not use MYD88, instead recruiting TRIF directly to activate IRF3-dependent interferon responses (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 3-5).

3.2 Downstream Transcriptional Programs

MYD88-dependent signaling activates multiple transcription factor families:

NF-κB Pathway: IRAK1 activation leads to TRAF6-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination and activation of TAK1. TAK1 phosphorylates the IKK complex, which phosphorylates IκBα, triggering its proteasomal degradation and releasing NF-κB dimers (p50/p65) to translocate to the nucleus and induce inflammatory gene expression (vegivinti2023roleofinnate pages 1-3, song2024myd88andits pages 1-2, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 2-3).

MAPK/AP-1 Pathways: TAK1 also activates mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascades including ERK, JNK, and p38, leading to AP-1 transcription factor activation and expression of inflammatory mediators (song2024myd88andits pages 1-2, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 2-3, pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 6-7).

Interferon Regulatory Factor Signaling: MYD88 can modulate interferon responses through multiple mechanisms. In plasmacytoid dendritic cells, TLR7 and TLR9 signaling recruits IRF7 to the myddosome, promoting type I interferon production (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, song2024myd88andits pages 1-2). MYD88 also regulates IRF5 activation in certain cell types (rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6, pereira2023regulationofinnate pages 6-7). Additionally, the MyD88 intermediate domain can mediate IRF-7 activity independently of death-domain folding (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4, song2024myd88andits pages 1-2).

Functional Outputs: These transcriptional programs induce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1β), chemokines, type I and type III interferons, acute-phase proteins, and enzymes such as inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) and cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4, rughetti2024imperativeroleof pages 5-6).

4. Recent Structural and Mechanistic Advances (2023-2024)

4.1 TIR Domain Higher-Order Assembly

A major advance in 2024 came from combined microcrystal electron diffraction (MicroED) and serial femtosecond crystallography studies that resolved MyD88 TIR-domain assemblies at near-atomic resolution (bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 7-8, bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 5-7, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 1-2). These structures revealed that:

  • MyD88 TIR domains assemble into two-stranded parallel filaments with head-to-tail contacts (bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 7-8, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 8-11)
  • TLR2 TIR domains can directly nucleate MyD88 assembly at 2.85 Å resolution, whereas TLR1 and TLR6 TIR domains cannot do so independently (li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 1-2, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 8-11, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 5-8)
  • Assembly involves conformational changes in the BB loop, CD loop, and B helix relative to monomeric structures (li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 8-11, li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 5-8)
  • Structure-guided mutagenesis confirmed that the BE and BCD interfaces observed crystallographically correspond to functionally relevant signaling interfaces in cells (bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 7-8)

These findings support a nucleated hierarchical assembly model termed "signaling by cooperative assembly formation" (SCAF), in which receptor clustering overcomes the energetic barrier to forming open-ended TIR-domain assemblies that recruit downstream effectors (bhatt2024structuralcharacterizationof pages 8-10).

4.2 Post-Translational Regulation

Recent studies (2023-2024) have identified regulatory mechanisms that fine-tune MyD88 activity:

Phosphorylation: A 2023 study demonstrated that MyD88 serine 257 (S257) phosphorylation promotes MyD88 aggregation, IRAK1 phosphorylation, and NF-κB activation. The oncogenic L265P mutation genocopies this phosphorylation-induced activation (minderman2023theoncogenichuman pages 8-9).

Acetylation: A 2024 study showed that upon LPS stimulation, the lysine acetyltransferase CBP acetylates TIR domains in the TLR4 signalosome, including MyD88, enhancing NF-κB signaling while having minimal effect on IRF3 pathways (saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 4-5).

Ubiquitination: OTUD5 deubiquitinase cleaves K11-linked polyubiquitin chains on MyD88 at Lys95, Lys231, and Lys250, enhancing MyD88 oligomerization and myddosome formation after LPS stimulation (li2024microcrystalelectrondiffraction pages 8-11).

5. Clinical Significance and Disease Associations

5.1 Oncogenic MYD88 L265P Mutation

Disease / clinical setting MYD88 alteration and reported frequency Biological or diagnostic significance Prognostic / therapeutic implications
Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) / lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma L265P in >90% of patients; approximately 91% in one review, leaving 5–10% MYD88-wild-type (WT) (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5) Hallmark driver and useful diagnostic biomarker, although not disease-specific. Constitutive MYD88 signaling promotes IRAK/BTK, NF-κB, BCL2, and tumor-cell survival pathways (tu2024lymphoplasmacyticlymphomawaldenströmmacroglobulinemia pages 7-9, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4) Genotype informs treatment selection, particularly expected response to BTK-pathway inhibition. WT disease has been associated with reduced response to some BTK inhibitors, greater transformation risk, and shorter overall survival (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2)
WM: mutant versus WT molecular phenotype A 2024 single-cell study analyzed five L265P, two WT, and two healthy-donor samples; L265P occurs in >90% of WM overall (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2) L265P and WT tumors exhibit distinct transcriptional programs involving NF-κB, BCL2, and BTK, with substantial intratumoral and interpatient heterogeneity Molecular heterogeneity may explain variable prognosis and treatment response even among L265P-positive patients; genotype alone does not capture all relevant tumor biology
IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (IgM-MGUS) L265P reported in approximately 50–80% of cases; one 2024 cohort found 60% (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5) May arise early in clonal evolution and helps distinguish IgM-MGUS/WM biology from IgM myeloma. It is associated with increased progression risk, although most carriers do not progress (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5) Potential risk-stratification biomarker, but insufficient alone to predict progression; additional genomic and clinical variables are required
IgM multiple myeloma and non-IgM MGUS L265P is generally absent from IgM myeloma and IgG/IgA MGUS (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5) Absence helps distinguish plasma-cell neoplasia from WM/LPL when clinicopathologic findings overlap; IgM myeloma is more often associated with t(11;14) Useful primarily for differential diagnosis rather than prognosis
Activated B-cell-like diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (ABC-DLBCL) Recurrent activating MYD88 mutations, especially L265P; uncommon in germinal-center B-cell-like DLBCL, but no single frequency applies across cohorts (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4) Constitutive MYD88–IRAK–NF-κB signaling supports lymphoma-cell growth and survival; some tumors are functionally dependent on mutant MYD88 (minderman2023theoncogenichuman pages 8-9) Establishes a targetable dependency involving the myddosome, IRAK kinases, BTK, and NF-κB. Prognostic effects vary by anatomic site, molecular subtype, and treatment context
Primary CNS, primary testicular, and other immune-privileged-site DLBCL MYD88 mutations, including L265P, are enriched, although frequencies were not quantified in the reviewed evidence (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4, minderman2023theoncogenichuman pages 8-9) Supports a shared oncogenic program centered on chronic MYD88 signaling and helps classify these extranodal lymphomas May provide diagnostic support and identify patients for pathway-directed therapy; clinical value remains context-dependent
Primary cutaneous DLBCL, leg type L265P is described as frequent and clinically relevant, without a numerical frequency in the reviewed evidence (tu2024lymphoplasmacyticlymphomawaldenströmmacroglobulinemia pages 7-9, tu2024lymphoplasmacyticlymphomawaldenströmmacroglobulinemia pages 9-11) Supports classification as a MYD88-driven lymphoma and may help distinguish it from other cutaneous B-cell neoplasms Reported to carry prognostic value, but its direction and magnitude require interpretation within disease-specific cohorts
Marginal-zone lymphoma (MZL), particularly IgM-secreting cases L265P occurs in a minority of cases; prevalence varies by MZL subtype (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5) Demonstrates that L265P is not specific to WM; mutation results must be integrated with morphology, immunophenotype, paraprotein, and clinical distribution Limited standalone prognostic value; used principally in differential diagnosis with other disease features
Other mature B-cell neoplasms Lower-frequency MYD88 mutations occur in chronic lymphocytic leukemia and splenic MZL; they are rare in hairy-cell leukemia, Burkitt lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma and appear absent from some entities such as primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5) MYD88 activation is concentrated in particular B-cell differentiation states and lymphoma subtypes rather than being a universal cancer event Clinical significance is disease-specific; low prevalence limits use as a universal prognostic biomarker
Non-L265P MYD88-mutant IgM gammopathies / lymphomas Reported variants include M232T, S243N, S222R, T294P, and S219C; frequencies are low or incompletely defined (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4) Some variants may activate MYD88 signaling, but their functional strength and diagnostic specificity are less established than those of L265P These variants should not automatically be interpreted as equivalent to L265P; functional annotation and disease context are necessary
MYD88-WT WM / IgM gammopathy Approximately 5–10% of WM lacks L265P or another detectable MYD88 mutation (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5) WT status does not exclude WM but may define a biologically distinct subgroup; exclusion of mimics and confirmation with sensitive testing are important Associated in several studies with greater transformation risk, resistance to some therapies, reduced BTK-inhibitor responsiveness, and shorter survival relative to mutant disease (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2)

Table: This table summarizes MYD88 alterations—especially L265P—across WM, DLBCL, related lymphomas, and precursor gammopathies. It compares reported frequencies, diagnostic relevance, and the clinical distinctions between MYD88-mutant and wild-type disease.

The most clinically significant MYD88 alteration is the somatic L265P mutation (leucine to proline at position 265 in the TIR domain), which drives several B-cell malignancies:

Waldenström Macroglobulinemia (WM): The L265P mutation occurs in >90% of WM cases, a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma characterized by IgM monoclonal protein secretion (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5, lemasson2023bcellspecificexpression pages 1-6). This mutation serves as a key diagnostic biomarker and driver of disease pathogenesis (tu2024lymphoplasmacyticlymphomawaldenströmmacroglobulinemia pages 7-9, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4). The mutation promotes constitutive MYD88 aggregation, IRAK/BTK pathway activation, NF-κB signaling, and B-cell survival (tu2024lymphoplasmacyticlymphomawaldenströmmacroglobulinemia pages 7-9, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4, minderman2023theoncogenichuman pages 8-9).

Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL): L265P is enriched in activated B-cell-like (ABC) DLBCL and is particularly frequent in primary CNS, primary testicular, and primary cutaneous DLBCL leg-type (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4, song2024myd88andits pages 2-4, tu2024lymphoplasmacyticlymphomawaldenströmmacroglobulinemia pages 9-11, minderman2023theoncogenichuman pages 8-9). The mutation creates oncogenic addiction to MYD88-IRAK-BTK-NF-κB signaling (minderman2023theoncogenichuman pages 8-9).

IgM Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (IgM-MGUS): L265P is present in 50-80% of IgM-MGUS cases and is associated with increased risk of progression to WM, although most carriers do not progress (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5).

5.2 Clinical and Therapeutic Implications

MYD88 Wild-Type Disease: Approximately 5-10% of WM patients lack the L265P mutation. MYD88 wild-type (WT) WM is associated with higher risk of transformation to aggressive lymphoma, reduced responsiveness to BTK inhibitors, and shorter overall survival compared to L265P-positive disease (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 1-2, bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 4-5).

Molecular Heterogeneity: A 2024 single-cell RNA sequencing study of WM patients revealed substantial intra-tumor and inter-patient transcriptional heterogeneity even among L265P-positive cases, with distinct gene expression signatures affecting NF-κB, BCL2, and BTK pathways (bagratuni2023myd88wildtype pages 2-4).

Therapeutic Targeting: The central role of MYD88 in lymphoma cell survival has prompted development of targeted therapies, including:
- Small molecule inhibitors of MYD88 dimerization (e.g., ST2825) that disrupt myddosome assembly (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4)
- BTK inhibitors (e.g., ibrutinib) that target downstream signaling in MYD88-mutant tumors
- Compounds targeting the TIR domain BB-loop interactions to reduce inflammatory signaling (saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 2-4, saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 4-5)

5.3 Role in Inflammatory Diseases

Beyond cancer, excessive MYD88 signaling contributes to various inflammatory conditions. Targeting MYD88 has shown promise in preclinical models of:
- Rheumatoid arthritis, where ST2825 reduced synovial fibroblast proliferation and invasiveness (song2024myd88andits pages 2-4)
- Sepsis and acute lung injury, where MYD88 inhibition modulated cytokine storm responses (saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 2-4)
- Viral infections including SARS-CoV-2, where MYD88 upregulation may impair type I interferon responses (saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 2-4, saikh2024targetingmyeloiddifferentiation pages 4-5)

6. Summary and Current Understanding

Human MYD88 functions as a pivotal cytoplasmic adaptor protein in innate immunity, linking activated pattern-recognition receptors to inflammatory signaling cascades. Its primary role is to scaffold the myddosome, a supramolecular signaling complex that amplifies receptor-derived signals through IRAK kinases, TRAF6, and downstream NF-κB, MAPK, and IRF pathways. MYD88 does not possess enzymatic activity or substrate specificity in the traditional sense; rather, it organizes proximity-driven protein interactions that enable signal transduction.

The protein's modular domain architecture—comprising an N-terminal death domain, intermediate domain, and C-terminal TIR domain—supports sequential receptor engagement, oligomerization, and kinase recruitment. Recent structural advances in 2024 have provided near-atomic resolution views of TIR-domain assembly, revealing the molecular basis for cooperative signaling complex formation.

Clinically, the oncogenic L265P mutation in the TIR domain drives >90% of Waldenström macroglobulinemia cases and substantial fractions of aggressive B-cell lymphomas, establishing MYD88 as both a diagnostic biomarker and therapeutic target. Current research focuses on developing selective inhibitors of MYD88 dimerization and downstream signaling to treat both malignant and inflammatory diseases.

The evidence presented here derives primarily from peer-reviewed publications from 2022-2024, with particular emphasis on recent structural, mechanistic, and clinical studies that have advanced understanding of MYD88 biology and its role in human disease.

📚 Additional Documentation

Notes

(MYD88-notes.md)

MYD88 (human, Q99836) review notes

Status of inputs

  • UniProt, GOA (236 rows, 229 seeded annotations after de-duplication) and all 63 GOA PMIDs were
    cached before review. Two extra PMIDs were fetched to trace mouse-sourced IEA rows
    (PMID:18319258, PMID:31164412).
  • Falcon deep research had not been produced when the review was drafted (MYD88 was queued behind
    the TLR batch); see the end of this file for its status.

Biology summary (with provenance)

  • MYD88 is a cytosolic TIR-domain adaptor with an N-terminal death domain (DD), an intermediate
    domain and a C-terminal TIR domain. It couples IL-1 receptor family and TLR receptors to the IRAK
    kinases. PMID:9430229 PMID:9430229
  • General adaptor for the Toll/IL-1R family. PMID:9734363
  • Recruitment to TLR4 (and TLR2) needs the bridging adaptor TIRAP, which is targeted to PIP2 at the
    plasma membrane. PMID:16751103 PMID:17258210
  • DD-mediated oligomerisation builds the Myddosome with IRAK4 and IRAK1/2. PMID:36865541 PMID:36865541 Endogenous MyD88 forms barrel-like scaffolds
    PMID:38961291
  • IRAK4 variants in the DD lose MyD88 binding PMID:24316379
  • Endosomal TLR7/8/9: MyD88–IRF7 complex drives IFN-alpha PMID:15361868; TLR9 phosphorylation is needed for MyD88 recruitment
    PMID:40980882; TLR8 in human macrophages PMID:33718825.
  • IL-1 family receptors: IL-1R, IL-18R, IL-33R all use MyD88 PMID:36865541; IL-33-driven human/mouse T cell
    polarisation needs MyD88 PMID:18802081.
  • Non-TIR receptor: TACI binds MyD88 PMID:20676093.
  • Regulation by ubiquitin: OTUD5 PMID:38605168; USP3 PMID:37971847.
  • Human genetics: MyD88 deficiency phenocopies IRAK-4 deficiency PMID:21057262.

Curation decisions and problems found

  1. GO:0008063 Toll signaling pathway (IBA and rat-sourced IEA). GO:0008063 is defined for
    ligand binding to "the receptor Toll" and is NOT an ancestor of GO:0002224 toll-like receptor
    signaling pathway (checked in OLS). The IBA node PTN000386853 spans fly Myd88 and vertebrate
    MYD88; the ancestral adaptor role is sound, but for a vertebrate the pathway is the TLR/IL-1R
    pathway. MODIFY to GO:0002755. This is the project's Toll-vs-TLR conflation issue on an adaptor.
  2. GO:0005121 Toll binding (rat IEA) — same issue; MODIFY to GO:0035325 Toll-like receptor
    binding.
  3. ATP-dependent histone chaperone activity / chromatin organization / chromatin remodeling (IEA)
    — traced to mouse Myd88 IMP from PMID:18319258, which shows only that MyD88 signaling is required
    for nucleosome remodeling at secondary-response promoters ("MyD88 is required for nucleosome
    remodeling and histone H3K4 trimethylation at secondary response promoters"). This is an indirect
    downstream effect; MYD88 has no histone chaperone activity. REMOVE all three. (Source defect is
    on the mouse Myd88 MGI annotation; no mouse review exists in this repo.)
  4. GO:0005123 death receptor binding (TAS PMID:9374458) — MYD88 binds IL-1R, not TNFR-family
    death receptors. MODIFY to GO:0005149 interleukin-1 receptor binding.
  5. Phagocytosis (IMP PMID:30883606) — the paper states "MyD88 silencing did not significantly
    reduce phagocytosis of either E. coli or S. aureus" in human macrophages; only mouse Myd88-/-
    iBMDMs showed reduced E. coli uptake. MARK_AS_OVER_ANNOTATED.
  6. Cellular response to mechanical stimulus (IEP PMID:19593445) — the cited full text (BAD in
    prostate cancer) contains no mention of MyD88 or mechanical stimulation. Likely a wrong PMID;
    UNDECIDED rather than REMOVE, flagged in reference_review.
    6b. Nucleus (EXP PMID:21057262) — no localisation data found in the cached clinical paper;
    kept as non-core (deferring to the curator) for consistency with the other nucleus rows.
  7. Cell surface (IDA PMID:22851693) — MYD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor; the paper studies
    membrane-associated IL-1R complex I. MODIFY to GO:0031234.
  8. protein binding IPI rows — MODIFY to TIR domain binding (TIRAP, SARM1, TLR partners in MAPPIT),
    Toll-like receptor binding (TLR2/TLR4 co-IP), death domain binding (FADD, IRAK4 DD–DD), protein
    kinase binding (IRAK1/IRAK4), TNFR superfamily binding (TACI); REMOVE for high-throughput screens
    with incidental partners, pathogen proteins and regulators (SPOP, STAP2, HDAC6, DOCK8, DHX9/36,
    TcpB, HCV NS5A).
  9. Type I interferon-mediated signaling pathway (IMP PMID:23633945) — the miR-21 paper measures
    IFN effector genes downstream of HCV-induced type I IFN production; MYD88 acts in the TLR arm
    that produces IFN, not in IFNAR signaling. MARK_AS_OVER_ANNOTATED (keep the sibling
    GO:0032481 positive regulation of type I interferon production as non-core).
  10. NLRP3 inflammasome complex assembly (NAS, IRAK review) — MYD88 does not assemble NLRP3; it
    primes/licenses via TLR signaling. MODIFY to GO:1900227 positive regulation of NLRP3
    inflammasome complex assembly (which is also separately supported by IMP PMID:33718825).

Deep research

  • Falcon deep research completed after the first draft (MYD88-deep-research-falcon.md). It is
    consistent with the review: direct TIR recruitment by TLR5/7/8/9, IL-1R and IL-18R; progressive
    MyD88 oligomerisation to a threshold before stable IRAK4 engagement; OTUD5 K11-chain cleavage;
    S257 phosphorylation and the oncogenic L265P TIR mutation. It reports nothing supporting
    histone-chaperone, chromatin or phagocytosis roles. Added as a reference and cited in the IL-1R
    family core function.

NEW annotations considered

  • GO:0035655 interleukin-18-mediated signaling pathway: UniProt states involvement; supported in
    review PMID:36865541 (IL-18R uses MyD88). MYD88 performs the adaptor step in IL-18R signaling
    (participation test passes: it is the adaptor that bridges IL-18R1 TIR to IRAK4). Comparator:
    QuickGO (2026-09-30) shows human GO:0035655 annotations only on IL18, IL18R1, IL18RAP, AKT1,
    PIK3R1, PDGFB — not on IRAK4, TRAF6 or mouse Myd88. The adaptor layer is systematically absent,
    so per CLAUDE.md this was NOT added as NEW; raised as a suggested question instead.

taxon:
  id: NCBITaxon:9606
  label: Homo sapiens
description: MYD88 (myeloid differentiation primary response protein 88) is a cytosolic signaling adaptor
  of the Toll-like receptor (TLR) and interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R) families. It has an N-terminal death
  domain, a short intermediate domain and a C-terminal TIR domain. Ligand-activated TLRs (all except TLR3)
  and IL-1, IL-18, IL-33 and IL-36 receptors recruit MYD88 through TIR-TIR contacts, either directly or
  via the bridging adaptor TIRAP at the plasma membrane (TLR2, TLR4). At endosomes it serves TLR7, TLR8
  and TLR9. MYD88 death domains then oligomerise and recruit IRAK4 and IRAK1/IRAK2 into a helical signaling
  platform, the Myddosome. In the Myddosome IRAK4 is activated and TRAF6 is engaged, which leads to NF-kappa-B
  and MAP kinase activation, inflammatory cytokine production and, in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, IRF7-dependent
  type I interferon production. MYD88 has no known enzymatic activity. It is regulated by K63- and K11-linked
  ubiquitination and by deubiquitinases such as USP3 and OTUD5. Inherited MYD88 deficiency causes susceptibility
  to pyogenic bacterial infection. The recurrent somatic L265P mutation constitutively activates the pathway
  in B-cell lymphomas.

- term:
    id: GO:0006325
    label: chromatin organization
  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000107
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:
  - UniProtKB:P22366
  - ensembl:ENSMUSP00000035092
  review:
    summary: Ensembl transfer (from mouse) of chromatin organization.
    action: REMOVE
    reason: The mouse source (IMP, PMID:18319258) shows MyD88-dependent signaling is needed for nucleosome
      remodeling at secondary-response promoters. That is a downstream effect of NF-kappaB signaling;
      MYD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor and does not organise chromatin.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:18319258
      supporting_text: This selective dependence correlates with the fact that MyD88 is required for nucleosome
        remodeling and histone H3K4 trimethylation at secondary response promoters
- term:
    id: GO:0006338
    label: chromatin remodeling
  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000108
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:
  - GO:0140674
  review:
    summary: Inter-ontology inference of chromatin remodeling from the histone chaperone MF.
    action: REMOVE
    reason: Inferred from GO:0140674, which is itself unsupported (see that row). MYD88 does not remodel
      chromatin.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:18319258
      supporting_text: This selective dependence correlates with the fact that MyD88 is required for nucleosome
        remodeling and histone H3K4 trimethylation at secondary response promoters
- term:
    id: GO:0006909
    label: phagocytosis
  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000107
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:
  - UniProtKB:P22366
  - ensembl:ENSMUSP00000035092
  review:
    summary: Ensembl transfer (from mouse) of phagocytosis.
    action: MARK_AS_OVER_ANNOTATED
    reason: MYD88 is not a phagocytic machinery component; effects on uptake are indirect and inconsistent
      (human macrophage siRNA shows no effect).
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:30883606
      supporting_text: MyD88 silencing did not significantly reduce phagocytosis of either E. coli or
        S. aureus (Fig 3A and 3B).
- term:
    id: GO:0006909
    label: phagocytosis
  evidence_type: IMP
  original_reference_id: PMID:30883606
  qualifier: involved_in
  review:
    summary: IMP from the TRAM/phagocytosis paper.
    action: MARK_AS_OVER_ANNOTATED
    reason: The paper reports that MyD88 silencing did not significantly reduce phagocytosis in human
      macrophages; only mouse Myd88-deficient iBMDMs showed reduced E. coli uptake. The claim is weak
      and indirect for human MYD88.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:30883606
      supporting_text: MyD88 silencing did not significantly reduce phagocytosis of either E. coli or
        S. aureus (Fig 3A and 3B).
    - reference_id: PMID:30883606
      supporting_text: Tlr4-/- mouse macrophages showed impaired uptake of E. coli, however, with less
        efficiency compared to TRAM- or Myd88-deficient macrophages (S5I Fig).
- term:
    id: GO:0006915
    label: apoptotic process
  evidence_type: IMP
  original_reference_id: PMID:22155231
  qualifier: involved_in
  review:
    summary: 'IMP: overexpressed MyD88 death domain shows early signs of apoptosis.'
    action: KEEP_AS_NON_CORE
    reason: Apoptosis via FADD/caspase-8 is an overexpression-driven side output of MYD88, not a core
      function.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:22155231
      supporting_text: In contrast, the isolated DD of MyD88 is more excluded from the nucleus, and its
        overexpression shows early signs of apoptosis.
    - reference_id: PMID:10880445
      supporting_text: TLR2 signals for apoptosis through MyD88 via a pathway involving Fas-associated
        death domain protein (FADD) and caspase 8.
- term:
    id: GO:0007165
    label: signal transduction
  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000002
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:
  - InterPro:IPR000157
  - InterPro:IPR000488
  - InterPro:IPR034249
  review:
    summary: 'InterPro IEA: signal transduction.'
    action: MODIFY
    reason: Correct but very general; the specific process is MyD88-dependent TLR signaling.
    proposed_replacement_terms:
    - id: GO:0002755
      label: MyD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling pathway
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:9734363
      supporting_text: We now demonstrate that signaling by the human Toll receptor employs an adaptor
        protein, MyD88, and induces activation of NF-kappaB via the Pelle-like kinase IRAK and the TRAF6
        protein, similar to IL-1R-mediated NF-kappaB activation.
- term:
    id: GO:0007165
    label: signal transduction
  evidence_type: NAS
  original_reference_id: PMID:9013863
  qualifier: involved_in
  review:
    summary: 'NAS from the cloning paper: death domain overexpression activates the IL-8 promoter.'
    action: MODIFY
    reason: Too general; replace with the MyD88-dependent TLR pathway (IL-1 pathway is carried separately).
    proposed_replacement_terms:
    - id: GO:0002755
      label: MyD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling pathway
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:9013863
      supporting_text: Overexpression of the death domain region leads to transcriptional activation of
        the IL-8 promoter.
- term:
    id: GO:0007166
    label: cell surface receptor signaling pathway
  evidence_type: TAS
  original_reference_id: PMID:9374458
  qualifier: involved_in
  review:
    summary: TAS cell surface receptor signaling pathway (IL-1R signaling complex).
    action: MODIFY
    reason: The cited work is about IL-1R signaling; replace with interleukin-1-mediated signaling pathway.
    proposed_replacement_terms:
    - id: GO:0070498
      label: interleukin-1-mediated signaling pathway
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:9374458
      supporting_text: Both associate with the IL-1R signaling complex.
- term:
    id: GO:0007249
    label: canonical NF-kappaB signal transduction
  evidence_type: NAS
  original_reference_id: PMID:38605168
  qualifier: involved_in
  review:
    summary: 'NAS: MyD88 oligomerization leads to NF-kappaB activation.'
    action: KEEP_AS_NON_CORE
    reason: NF-kappaB activation is the main downstream output, but the canonical NF-kappaB cascade proper
      (IKK activation, IkB degradation) is carried out by TRAF6/TAK1/IKK downstream of MYD88.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:38605168
      supporting_text: This polyubiquitin cleavage enhances MyD88 oligomerization after LPS stimulation,
        which subsequently promotes the recruitment of downstream IRAK4 and IRAK2 to form Myddosome and
        the activation of NF-κB and MAPK signaling and production of inflammatory cytokines.
- term:
    id: GO:0007254
    label: JNK cascade
  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000107
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:
  - UniProtKB:Q6Y1S1
  - ensembl:ENSRNOP00000018341
  review:
    summary: 'Ensembl transfer (rat): JNK cascade.'
    action: KEEP_AS_NON_CORE
    reason: JNK activation is a downstream output of MyD88-dependent signalling, not a step MYD88 performs.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:38605168
      supporting_text: This polyubiquitin cleavage enhances MyD88 oligomerization after LPS stimulation,
        which subsequently promotes the recruitment of downstream IRAK4 and IRAK2 to form Myddosome and
        the activation of NF-κB and MAPK signaling and production of inflammatory cytokines.
- term:
    id: GO:0008063
    label: Toll signaling pathway
  evidence_type: IBA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000033
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:
  - FB:FBgn0033402
  - PANTHER:PTN000386853
  - RGD:735043
  review:
    summary: 'IBA (PTN000386853, donors fly Myd88 and rat Myd88): Toll signaling pathway.'
    action: MODIFY
    reason: GO:0008063 is defined for ligand binding to "the receptor Toll" and is not an ancestor of
      GO:0002224 toll-like receptor signaling pathway (checked in OLS). The IBD at the MyD88 node correctly
      captures an ancestral adaptor role in Toll-family receptor signaling, but human MYD88 functions
      downstream of vertebrate TLRs and IL-1R family receptors, not Toll. The vertebrate-appropriate term
      is GO:0002755.
    proposed_replacement_terms:
    - id: GO:0002755
      label: MyD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling pathway
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:9734363
      supporting_text: We now demonstrate that signaling by the human Toll receptor employs an adaptor
        protein, MyD88, and induces activation of NF-kappaB via the Pelle-like kinase IRAK and the TRAF6
        protein, similar to IL-1R-mediated NF-kappaB activation.
    - reference_id: PMID:36865541
      supporting_text: Signaling via most TLRs and IL-1Rs is mediated by the protein myeloid differentiation
        primary-response protein 88 (MyD88).
    propagation_review:
      root_cause: TERM_SCOPING_PROBLEM
      failure_modes:
      - LINEAGE_OR_TAXON_MISMATCH
      - GRANULARITY_MISMATCH
      source_entities:
      - source_id: PANTHER:PTN000386853
        source_label: PTN000386853
        source_status: SUPPORTS_SOURCE_BUT_NOT_TARGET
        comment: The MyD88-family node carries both GO:0008063 (seeded from fly Myd88 and rat Myd88) and
          the vertebrate TLR terms. The ancestral adaptor role in Toll-family receptor signalling is sound,
          but GO:0008063 names the Drosophila Toll receptor pathway and is not an ancestor of GO:0002224,
          so for vertebrate descendants the TLR pathway term is the correct scope.
- term:
    id: GO:0008063
    label: Toll signaling pathway
  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000107
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:

  - ensembl:ENSRNOP00000018341
  review:
    summary: Ensembl transfer (rat) of Toll signaling pathway.
    action: MODIFY
    reason: 'As for the IBA row: GO:0008063 is the Drosophila Toll pathway; for human MYD88 use the MyD88-dependent

    proposed_replacement_terms:
    - id: GO:0002755
      label: MyD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling pathway
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:9734363
      supporting_text: We now demonstrate that signaling by the human Toll receptor employs an adaptor
        protein, MyD88, and induces activation of NF-kappaB via the Pelle-like kinase IRAK and the TRAF6
        protein, similar to IL-1R-mediated NF-kappaB activation.
- term:
    id: GO:0009617
    label: response to bacterium
  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000117
  qualifier: involved_in
  supporting_entities:
  - ARBA:ARBA00026494
  review:
    summary: 'ARBA: response to bacterium.'
    action: KEEP_AS_NON_CORE
    reason: True at organism level (MyD88 deficiency causes pyogenic bacterial infections) but downstream
      of the core signalling role.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:21057262
      supporting_text: The clinical features of IRAK-4 and MyD88 deficiency were indistinguishable.
- term:
    id: GO:0009986
    label: cell surface
  evidence_type: IDA
  original_reference_id: PMID:22851693
  qualifier: is_active_in
  review:
    summary: IDA cell surface in the IL-1 complex I membrane-translocation study.
    action: MODIFY
    reason: MYD88 has no extracellular part; the study examines membrane-bound receptor complexes on the
      cytoplasmic side. Replace with extrinsic component of cytoplasmic side of plasma membrane.
    proposed_replacement_terms:
    - id: GO:0031234
      label: extrinsic component of cytoplasmic side of plasma membrane
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:22851693
      supporting_text: It is important to note that the modified IRAK1 is always membrane associated and
        detected in membrane-bound receptor complex I and II

        the activation of NF-κB and MAPK signaling and production of inflammatory cytokines.

  evidence_type: IEA
  original_reference_id: GO_REF:0000107
  qualifier: enables
  supporting_entities:

  - ensembl:ENSMUSP00000035092
  review:
    summary: 'Ensembl transfer (mouse): ATP-dependent histone chaperone activity.'
    action: REMOVE
    reason: The mouse source is an IMP from PMID:18319258 showing that MyD88 signalling is required for
      nucleosome remodeling at secondary-response promoters. That is an indirect transcriptional consequence;
      MYD88 is a cytoplasmic adaptor with no ATPase or histone-binding activity. The molecular-function
      annotation (and its inferred chromatin-remodeling process) is a misapplication of a phenotype.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:18319258
      supporting_text: This selective dependence correlates with the fact that MyD88 is required for nucleosome
        remodeling and histone H3K4 trimethylation at secondary response promoters

  evidence_type: IMP
  original_reference_id: PMID:33718825
  qualifier: involved_in
  review:
    summary: 'IMP: TLR8/MYD88 required for NLRP3 activation by viral GU-rich RNA.'
    action: KEEP_AS_NON_CORE
    reason: MYD88 supplies the TLR8 priming signal; a regulatory, non-core role.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:33718825
      supporting_text: With the use of inhibitors and RNAi, we also demonstrate that activation of the
        NLRP3 inflammasome by GU-rich RNA is specifically TLR8-dependent and RNA-mediated, leading to
        CASP1 activation and the conversion of pro-IL-1β to its active form.
    - reference_id: PMID:33718825

        and IL-6 expression from human macrophages
- term:
    id: GO:1902554
    label: serine/threonine protein kinase complex
  evidence_type: NAS
  original_reference_id: PMID:30256449
  qualifier: part_of
  review:
    summary: 'NAS (Myddosome review): serine/threonine protein kinase complex.'
    action: ACCEPT
    reason: The Myddosome contains the IRAK4 and IRAK1/2 kinases with MYD88 as its scaffold; GO has no
      specific Myddosome term, so this is the most specific available complex term.
    supported_by:
    - reference_id: PMID:30256449
      supporting_text: Upon activation, TLRs facilitate the assembly of large intracellular oligomeric
        signaling complexes, termed Myddosomes, which initiate key signal transduction pathways to elicit
        critical inflammatory immune responses.
    - reference_id: PMID:36865541
      supporting_text: The myddosome is a supramolecular signaling complex assembled upon dimerization
        of IL-1Rs and most TLRs (except TLR3), and is composed of MyD88, IRAK4, IRAK1 and/or IRAK2, in
        addition to TRAF6.

core_functions:
- description: 'Signaling adaptor that couples ligand-activated TLRs (all except TLR3) to the IRAK kinases:
    MYD88 is recruited through its TIR domain (directly, or via TIRAP for TLR2/TLR4) and nucleates the
    Myddosome through death-domain oligomerisation.'
  molecular_function:
    id: GO:0035591
    label: signaling adaptor activity
  directly_involved_in:
  - id: GO:0002755
    label: MyD88-dependent toll-like receptor signaling pathway
  locations:
  - id: GO:0031234
    label: extrinsic component of cytoplasmic side of plasma membrane
  - id: GO:0005829
    label: cytosol

suggested_questions:
- question: Should GO:0008063 Toll signaling pathway be removed from the MyD88-family IBD at PTN000386853
    for vertebrate descendants, or restricted to the arthropod clade? GO:0008063 is defined for the receptor
    Toll and is not an ancestor of GO:0002224, so all vertebrate MYD88 orthologues currently inherit a
    Drosophila-specific pathway term.
- question: Human MYD88 is the adaptor for IL-18R1/IL18RAP signalling, but neither human MYD88 nor IRAK4
    or TRAF6 is annotated to GO:0035655 interleukin-18-mediated signaling pathway (only ligand, receptor
    and a few kinases are). Is this a deliberate convention or a gap for the adaptor layer?
- question: The mouse Myd88 annotations to GO:0140674 ATP-dependent histone chaperone activity and GO:0006325
    chromatin organization (IMP, PMID:18319258) read an indirect transcriptional phenotype as a molecular
    activity; should the MGI source annotations be withdrawn so that they stop propagating to human and
    other orthologues?
- question: Which reference supports the IEP annotation to GO:0071260 cellular response to mechanical
    stimulus? The cited PMID:19593445 does not mention MyD88.
- question: Would a Myddosome cellular-component term (MYD88-IRAK4-IRAK1/2 helical assembly) be useful?
    GO:1902554 serine/threonine protein kinase complex is currently the most specific available term.
suggested_experiments:
- description: Endogenous-tag proteomics (as in PMID:38961291) comparing Myddosome composition after IL-18,
    IL-33 and IL-36 stimulation with TLR stimulation, to test whether the MYD88 scaffold recruits the
    same effector set across IL-1R family receptors.
- description: Genome-edited human macrophages lacking MYD88 (not siRNA), to test whether any phagocytosis
    defect exists independently of TLR4-TRAM signalling. Human siRNA and mouse knockout data currently
    disagree.
- description: Chromatin immunoprecipitation or CUT&RUN for endogenous MYD88, with a nuclear-exclusion
    mutant, to test whether the reported nuclear pool has any direct role at promoters or is an overexpression
    artefact.
